About this simulation

On screen
Top: the star's cross-section on a dark sky, centred on ξ = 0 and filled out to the stepping front, brighter where ρ/ρc = wnp is larger, with a crisp edge at the surface ξ1; the colour key in its corner gives ρ/ρc. Bottom: w against ξ on the same ξ axis, 0 to 16, drawn as the steps go out; finished runs stay as faint labelled curves with a tick at their ξ1. Inset: ρ/ρc against r/R, comparing stars of different index at the same radius R.
Controls
The polytropic index np, 0 to 4 in steps of 0.5; changing it returns the front to the centre and pauses. ▶ Play steps outwards at 2 units of ξ per second and stops at the surface. “Clear earlier runs” removes the faint earlier runs.
Measured
ξ and w are the current stepping front, from the engine's RK4 solution of the Lane–Emden equation; ξ1 and ρc/ρ̄ = ξ1/(3|dw/dξ|) at the surface appear once the front reaches it. All of these are in the Readouts panel of the sidebar.
Model
w is defined by ρ = ρcwnp, and ξ = r/rs with a length unit rs that depends on the index, Kp and ρc, so widths in ξ cannot be compared between indices; the inset compares shapes at the same radius. A polytrope assumes one pressure–density law throughout. Real stars follow one only roughly: np ≈ 1.5 fits fully convective stars and low-mass white dwarfs, and np = 3 is Eddington's standard model of a radiative star. For np ≥ 5 there is no surface at a finite ξ.
Stepping Out to the Surface of a Star
A star built step by stepcross-section above, w against ξ below

Guided Inquiry

1 · The index zero star

Set the polytropic index to np = 0. Before pressing play, predict how the brightness of the cross-section, which shows the density, will vary from the centre to the surface.

2 · Where index one ends

Keep the finished np = 0 curve on the plot and set np = 1. Before pressing play, predict where the new curve of w reaches zero compared with the first one.

3 · Where index three ends

Set np = 3. Before pressing play, predict where the curve of w reaches zero.

4 · Density halfway out

Keep the settings of question 3. In units of ξ the np = 3 star reaches almost three times as far as the np = 0 star: compare their ξ1 ticks. Before looking at the inset, where the stars are drawn to the same radius R, predict what fraction of its central density the np = 3 star has halfway out, at r = R/2.

5 · Central against mean density

Keep the settings of question 3 and read the ratio of central to mean density, about 54. Set np = 4. Before pressing play, predict that ratio for the new star.

6 · What you found

The surface of a polytrope is the first zero of w, at ξ1 = √6, π, 6.90 and 14.97 for np = 0, 1, 3 and 4. The larger the index, the softer the gas, the longer the tail in ξ and the more the mass is packed into the centre: ρc/ρ̄ = 1, 3.29, 54.2 and 622. Because rs differs for each index, only the same-radius view in the inset compares real shapes.

Stepping Out to the Surface of a Star

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A polytrope is a star with one pressure–density law all the way through. This sim steps its Lane–Emden equation outward from the centre, drawing the density profile as it goes, until the density reaches zero at the surface.

What you'll learn

  • How one pressure–density law becomes a single equation for the density.
  • Why the surface of a polytrope is the first zero of w.
  • How the index np sets where that zero falls.
  • How the index sets the way the mass is spread.
The sim's three views: cross-section, plot and inset.

What's on screen

  • Top: the star's cross-section, filled out to the stepping front. Brighter means denser; the key gives ρ/ρc.
  • Thin gold arc: the front. When the steps stop, it is the surface.
  • Cyan curve: w against ξ for the current run, drawn as the steps go out. The ξ axis runs from 0 to 16.
  • Faint grey curves: earlier finished runs, each with a labelled tick at its ξ1.
  • Inset: ρ/ρc against r/R, for stars of different index drawn to the same radius R.
See itLook at the three views and the Readouts panel. Watch for: the cross-section above, w against ξ below, the inset at the right, and Front ξ, Front w, Surface ξ1 and ρc/ρ̄ in the sidebar.

03

The surface is the first zero of w

A polytrope obeys one law, P = Kp ρ1+1/np (4.35). Write the density as ρ = ρc wnp, with w = 1 at the centre, and the radius as r = rs ξ, where rs absorbs the constants (4.38). Hydrostatic balance and mass continuity then reduce to the Lane–Emden equation (4.39):

The definitions (4.35) and (4.38), then eq. (4.39) below.
Eq. (4.39), the Lane–Emden equation. The right-hand side is the downward push on w.

At the centre w = 1 and dw/dξ = 0, because the pressure gradient vanishes where the enclosed mass is zero. The sim steps ξ outward from there in small increments. The surface is where the density first falls to zero, at the first zero ξ1 of w, so the radius is R = rs ξ1.

Any solution starts at w = 1 with zero slope; its first zero is the surface.
Key idea. The surface is not a radius you choose. It is where stepping outward first brings w to zero.
See itSet the index to 2.5 and press Play. Watch for: w starting at 1 with a flat slope, falling as the front moves out, and the front stopping where w reaches 0.
04

A uniform star ends at a crisp edge, ξ1 = √6

For np = 0 the right-hand side of (4.39) is −1, and ρ = ρc w0 = ρc wherever w > 0: the density is uniform. Integrating twice with the central conditions gives (4.40):

Eq. (4.40), the index-zero solution.

The curve w = 1 − ξ²/6 reaches zero at ξ1 = √6 = 2.449. The density then drops from ρc to zero at once, a crisp edge. The mean density equals ρc, so ρc/ρ̄ = 1.

Index zero: w reaches zero at √6 = 2.45; the density is uniform out to the edge.

The plot marks ξ1 as 2.45; the Surface ξ1 readout keeps three decimals, 2.449.

Key idea. An index-zero star does not fade out. Its density holds at ρc until the edge.
See itSet the index to 0 and press Play. Watch for: the brightness staying the same out to a sharp edge, w reaching 0 at ξ = 2.449, and ρc/ρ̄ reading 1.00.
05

Index one ends further out, at ξ1 = π

For np = 1 the equation is linear. With w = Θ/ξ it becomes d²Θ/dξ² = −Θ, whose solutions are sin ξ and cos ξ. Only Θ = sin ξ gives a w that is finite and equal to 1 at the centre, since sin ξ/ξ → 1 as ξ → 0. This is (4.41):

Eq. (4.41), the index-one solution.

Its first zero is π = 3.142, further out than √6 = 2.449. The reason is in (4.39): for 0 < w < 1 a higher power is a smaller number, so the push −wnp is weaker for np = 1 than for np = 0, and w falls more slowly.

Indices 0 and 1, as in the notes' Fig. 47. Both start at w = 1 with zero slope.
See itPress Play at index 1, with the index-zero run kept as a faint curve. Watch for: the new curve running past the faint index-zero curve and ending at a tick at 3.14, with Surface ξ1 reading 3.142.
06

A larger index pushes the first zero further out

The same reasoning holds all the way up: the larger np, the weaker the push where w < 1, and the longer the tail of w. The first zero is at ξ1 = 3.654 for np = 1.5 (the notes: ≈ 3.65), 6.897 for np = 3 (the notes: ≈ 6.90) and 14.972 for np = 4. For np = 5 it moves off to infinity, which is why the slider stops at 4.

w against ξ for indices 0, 1, 3 and 4, on the sim's 0 to 16 axis. Each ends at its first zero.

A long tail in ξ is not a large star. The unit rs depends on the index, Kp and ρc, so widths in ξ cannot be compared between indices. Only R = rs ξ1 is a radius.

See itSet the index to 3 and press Play, with the index 0 and 1 runs kept as faint curves. Watch for: the new curve passing both faint curves and carrying on, after a long shallow tail, to a tick at 6.90, with Surface ξ1 reading 6.897.
07

A larger index packs the mass toward the centre

The mass follows from (4.39) itself, because ξ² wnp is minus the derivative of ξ² dw/dξ. That gives (4.42). Dividing M by the volume of the sphere of radius R = rs ξ1 gives the ratio of central to mean density:

Eq. (4.42), and the ratio ρc/ρ̄. The slope is taken at the surface.

The ratio depends on the index alone, not on the mass. For np = 0 and 1 it is exactly 1 and π²/3. Drawn to the same radius R, the np = 3 star has w = 0.284 halfway out, so ρ/ρc = 0.023, against 1 for np = 0.

Key idea. At the same radius, the higher the index, the more of the mass sits near the centre.
See itSet the index to 3, then to 4, with the earlier runs kept as faint curves. Watch for: ρc/ρ̄ reading 54.18 at index 3 and 622.41 at index 4, and in the inset the index 3 curve down near zero by r/R = 0.5.
08

Where it matters

  • Fully convective stars. The temperature gradient is adiabatic, so P ∝ ργ with γ = 5/3 gives np = 3/2. At index 1.5 the sim reads ξ1 = 3.654 and ρc/ρ̄ = 5.99.
  • Eddington's model. If the pressure of radiation is the same fraction of the total everywhere, np = 3. Eddington used it in 1926, and it describes the Sun reasonably well. The notes put the Sun's central density at about a hundred times its mean; index 3 gives 54, the right order for a one-law model.
  • The limits of the idea. A polytrope assumes one law throughout. Real stars follow one only roughly, and above np = 5 there is no surface at all.
Go deeper: where the size of the star comes from

The index fixes the shape w(ξ). The scale comes from rs² = (np + 1) Kp ρc1/np − 1 / 4πG (4.38). For np = 1 the central density drops out, so R = π √(Kp/2πG) depends on neither the central density nor the mass. For other indices, (4.42) relates R to M (notes, problems 3 and 4).

09

Summary

In one line. A polytrope's surface is the first zero of the Lane–Emden solution w, so the index sets both where the star ends and how its mass is spread.
  • The surface is the first zero ξ1 of w in (4.39), and R = rs ξ1.
  • ξ1 = √6, π, 6.90 and 14.97 for np = 0, 1, 3 and 4; infinite at 5.
  • ρc/ρ̄ = ξ1 / (3|dw/dξ|) at the surface: 1, 3.29, 54.18 and 622.41.
  • ξ cannot be compared between indices; the same-radius inset can.

Common mix-ups

  • "Every curve ends at √6, because they all start at w = 1." The start is shared; the push −wnp is not, so the zero moves out.
  • "Reaching further in ξ means a more spread-out star." rs changes with the index; only the same-radius view compares shapes.
  • "ρc/ρ̄ is set by the mass." It is set by the index alone.

Things to try on your own

  • Index 2, press Play: Surface ξ1 should read 4.353 and ρc/ρ̄ 11.40.
  • Index 3.5, press Play: Surface ξ1 should read 9.536 and ρc/ρ̄ 152.89.
